questions.prompt: Lesson 1 walks through four points where the same vulnerability at Northbridge Retail could be caught. Put them in order from cheapest-to-fix to most expensive-and-risky.
items: A static analysis plugin flags a hardcoded database password as the developer types it in the editor
A teammate catches a missing input check on the checkout form during code review
An automated scan blocks a build in the CI/CD pipeline because a container image includes a package with a known critical vulnerability
A researcher or an attacker finds the same flaw live in production, after the checkout service is already processing real payment data
questions.explain: Lesson 1's whole point is that the same flaw costs more to fix the further right it travels on the delivery timeline: seconds in the editor, a commit in code review, a dependency bump in the pipeline, and a full incident response once it's live in production.

questions.prompt: Northbridge Retail's checkout service calls the payment processor's API over an unauthenticated internal network link, with no TLS enforced. Which STRIDE category from Lesson 2 does this threat belong to?
options: Tampering — without TLS, data in transit between checkout and the payment processor could be modified by anyone who can observe that link
Repudiation — because there's no audit trail proving the call happened
Denial of service — because an attacker could flood the unauthenticated connection
Elevation of privilege — because the call might reach an admin-only endpoint
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names this exact scenario: an unenforced-TLS payment processor call is a Tampering threat, since data in transit could be modified. The lesson's own fix is changing the call to run over TLS with mutual authentication — a design choice that's cheap on a whiteboard and expensive after deployment.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 3, select every OWASP Top 10 category the course specifically calls out as especially close to a DevOps/platform engineer's own daily tooling decisions.
options: Security Misconfiguration
Software Supply Chain Failures
Security Logging and Alerting Failures
Injection
Cryptographic Failures
questions.explain: Lesson 3 names three categories as especially close to the DevOps/platform role: Security Misconfiguration (infrastructure-as-code and container defaults), Software Supply Chain Failures (dependency and build-pipeline integrity), and Security Logging and Alerting Failures (observability and audit trail). Injection and Cryptographic Failures matter too, but the lesson frames them as closer to an application developer's daily work.

questions.prompt: Match each Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) stage to the concrete security activity Lesson 4 places at that stage.
right: Security requirements are defined alongside functional ones, such as "payment data must be encrypted at rest and in transit"
The architecture is threat modeled, using the STRIDE walkthrough from Lesson 2
Automated security testing runs in the pipeline: SAST, dependency scanning, secrets detection, and IaC scanning
The running environment itself is hardened — least-privilege identity and secrets pulled from a vault instead of baked into images
questions.explain: Lesson 4 maps a concrete activity to every SSDLC stage: Plan defines security requirements, Design is where threat modeling happens, Build/Test is where Chapter 4's automated scans run, and Deploy is where least-privilege identity and vault-sourced secrets harden the running environment.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 5, an identity's privilege level determines its ________ — how much damage is possible if that identity is ever compromised, misused, or simply makes a mistake.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 defines blast radius as the scope of potential damage from a compromised or misused identity — the reason a read-only credential leaking is a bounded problem while a broadly-scoped admin credential leaking can mean deleted infrastructure or exfiltrated data.

questions.prompt: In AWS IAM, what does a role's trust policy actually define, per Lesson 7?
options: Which principal is allowed to assume the role
Which AWS actions and resources the role can use once assumed
The password policy for any user who assumes the role
The maximum session duration for every IAM role in the account
Which S3 buckets in the account are publicly accessible
The rotation schedule for the role's temporary credentials
questions.explain: Lesson 7 is explicit that a role carries two separate documents: the trust policy (also called an assume-role policy) defines who is allowed to assume the role, and doesn't grant any AWS permissions by itself.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the permissions policy, the role's other half — it defines what the role can actually do once assumed, which is a completely separate document from the trust policy. Conflating the two, Lesson 7 warns, is a common source of confusion: a role can have a wide-open trust policy and a narrow permissions policy, or the reverse, and both halves matter independently.

questions.prompt: Northbridge Retail needs a monitoring agent that reads metrics from every namespace in the cluster. Per Lesson 8, which combination correctly grants this while still respecting least privilege?
options: A ClusterRole bound with a ClusterRoleBinding, since the need is genuinely cluster-wide
A namespaced Role bound with a separate RoleBinding created individually in every namespace
A ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding, scoped to just one namespace
No binding is needed at all, since ClusterRoles automatically apply everywhere without one
questions.explain: Lesson 8 reserves ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding for genuinely cluster-wide needs, naming exactly this example: a monitoring agent that reads metrics from every namespace. Day-to-day, single-service access should stay on namespaced Roles instead, which is the least-privilege default the lesson recommends.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about workload identity, per Lesson 9.
options: It replaces a long-lived stored credential with a short-lived, auto-rotating token issued through federation
Azure Workload Identity federates an AKS service account to a Microsoft Entra ID application
AWS IRSA federates an EKS service account to an IAM role through the cluster's OIDC provider
A workload identity token, once issued, never expires, which is what makes it secure
Workload identity eliminates the need for Kubernetes RBAC entirely
questions.explain: Workload identity's whole design is a short-lived, auto-rotating token in place of a stored secret, obtained through federation — Azure Workload Identity federates to an Entra ID application, AWS IRSA federates to an IAM role via OIDC. The token is deliberately short-lived, not permanent, and workload identity sits on top of Kubernetes RBAC (which still governs in-cluster access) rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Northbridge Retail's checkout pod reading from Azure Key Vault (Lesson 9's federated workload identity exchange) in the order they actually happen.
items: A pod using the federated service account starts, and Kubernetes automatically mounts a short-lived, auto-rotating token
The pod presents that token to Azure when it calls Key Vault
Azure verifies the token against the cluster's trusted OIDC issuer
Azure exchanges the verified token for temporary credentials scoped to the federated Key Vault Secrets User role
The pod uses those temporary credentials to read the payment processor's API key from the one vault that role allows
questions.explain: Lesson 9 walks through this exact chain: the pod's service account token is mounted automatically at startup, presented to Azure, verified against the trusted OIDC issuer, exchanged for temporary credentials scoped to exactly one Key Vault role, and only then used to read the secret — with nothing long-lived stored anywhere along the way.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 13, HashiCorp Vault organizes everything around ________ — pluggable components, each mounted at its own path, each handling a different kind of secret, such as the KV engine or the database engine.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 introduces secrets engines as Vault's core organizing concept — the KV engine is the general-purpose equivalent of a Key Vault secret, but Vault also ships a database engine, a PKI engine, and a transit engine, each mounted at its own API path.

questions.prompt: A Northbridge Retail developer commits an AWS access key, then deletes that line in the very next commit. Per Lesson 17, what's actually true about that key now?
options: It's still recoverable from git history, so the only real fix is to rotate the key and revoke the old credential at the source
Deleting the line in a later commit fully removes the key from the repository
The key is automatically invalidated the moment the line is deleted from the file
The key is safe to leave as-is, as long as the repository stays private
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is direct about this: deleting a committed secret in a later commit doesn't delete it from git history. Anyone who clones the repo, or scans historical commits, can still retrieve it — the only real fix is rotating the credential and revoking the old one at the source, treating the committed value as permanently compromised.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how secrets actually leak, per Lesson 10's four common patterns.
options: A secret committed to source control is still recoverable from git history even after the line is deleted in a later commit
A secret baked into a container image layer can be extracted by anyone who can pull that image
Logging a full configuration at startup can expose a secret to a centralized logging system with broader read access than the secret itself ever had
Telling developers "just don't commit it" fully solves secret sprawl, since it's purely a discipline problem
A secret pasted into a Slack message "just this once" is automatically rotated within 24 hours
questions.explain: Lesson 10 names committed-to-source-control, baked-into-an-image, logged-in-plaintext, and shared-out-of-band as the four common leak patterns, and explicitly argues that "just don't commit it" treats a structural problem as a discipline failure — it isn't sufficient on its own. Nothing in Vault, GitHub, or Slack auto-rotates a credential just because it was pasted into a chat message.

questions.prompt: Match each secrets-management tool or pattern to the trait that most distinguishes it in Chapter 3.
right: Provides built-in, scheduled rotation, including managed rotation Lambdas for services like RDS and Redshift
Syncs a vault's secret into a Kubernetes Secret automatically, keeping the real vault as the source of truth
Hides a secret's value behind an explicit "Show Secret Value" click, with access gated by Azure RBAC
Cloud-agnostic, with pluggable secrets engines including one that issues dynamic, per-request database credentials
questions.explain: Key Vault's distinguishing detail from Lesson 11 is hiding values behind an explicit extra click, gated by Azure RBAC. Secrets Manager's signature feature (Lesson 12) is scheduled, often fully-managed rotation. Vault (Lesson 13) is cloud-agnostic with pluggable engines, including dynamic per-request database credentials. The External Secrets Operator (Lesson 14) syncs whichever vault is the real source of truth into a Kubernetes Secret automatically.

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of Software Composition Analysis (SCA), per Lesson 16?
options: Scanning third-party and open-source dependencies for known vulnerabilities, typically tracked as CVEs
Analyzing an application's own source code for vulnerability patterns without executing it
Scanning a fully-built container image's OS packages and application dependencies, layer by layer
Scanning infrastructure-as-code files for known misconfiguration patterns before deployment
Generating a signed inventory of every component in a software build
Detecting credential-shaped patterns in code and git history
questions.explain: Lesson 16 defines SCA as scanning manifest and lockfiles and comparing every dependency version against databases of known vulnerabilities (CVEs with a CVSS severity score) — treating the imported code as a black box rather than analyzing logic the team wrote.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes SAST (Lesson 15), not SCA. Lesson 16 is explicit that this is a different problem than SAST: SAST analyzes the logic a developer wrote, while SCA assumes imported code is a black box and only checks whether a specific package version is known to be vulnerable.

questions.code:
Check: CKV_AZURE_59: "Ensure that Storage accounts disallow public access"
    FAILED for resource: azurerm_storage_account.product_images
    File: /modules/storage/main.tf:12-24
questions.prompt: A Northbridge Retail engineer's Terraform defines a storage account without restricting public access, producing the Checkov finding above. Per Lesson 18, when should this scan actually catch the problem, and why does the timing matter?
options: Before `terraform apply` ever runs, against the plan, so the pull request fails and the storage account is never actually provisioned publicly
After `terraform apply`, by scanning the resource once it's already live
Only manually, since Checkov doesn't support scanning Terraform files
Timing doesn't matter here, since the fix is the same either way
questions.explain: Lesson 18 is specific that IaC scanning has to run before `apply`, against the plan — catching this in a running environment means the storage account was already public for however long it took someone to notice, exactly the "caught in production" scenario Lesson 1 warns is the most expensive place to find a flaw.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SBOMs and supply chain risk, per Lesson 19.
options: An SBOM is generated automatically as part of the CI pipeline, not hand-maintained in a spreadsheet
SPDX and CycloneDX are the two dominant SBOM formats
Supply chain risk also covers whether the build pipeline itself was compromised, not just whether a dependency has a CVE
An SBOM by itself proves a build artifact wasn't tampered with on the way to production
SBOMs are useful mainly during routine operations, not in the hours right after a new CVE is disclosed
questions.explain: Lesson 19 generates SBOMs automatically at build time in SPDX or CycloneDX format, and distinguishes what an SBOM proves from what provenance proves: the SBOM says what's in the box, while frameworks like SLSA and tools like Sigstore/cosign prove the box wasn't tampered with — an SBOM alone doesn't establish that. The lesson's whole framing is that SBOMs earn their keep specifically in the hours after a new CVE is disclosed, not mainly during routine operations.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a known vulnerability's severity is most commonly scored using ________, a numeric system from 0 to 10, while the vulnerability itself is tracked under a standardized identifier called a CVE.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 introduces CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) as the standardized identifier for a known vulnerability, paired with a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score used to prioritize which ones to fix first.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 4 scanning category to the specific tool named as its example.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 names CodeQL as the engine behind SAST (GitHub code scanning), Lesson 16 names Dependabot for dependency/composition scanning, Lesson 17 names gitleaks (alongside trufflehog) for secrets detection, and Lesson 18 names Checkov for IaC scanning.

questions.prompt: Northbridge Retail's checkout namespace is labeled `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. Per Lesson 21, what does this namespace-level enforcement actually guarantee about every pod created in it?
options: Every pod is required to run as non-root, with all Linux capabilities dropped by default and privilege escalation blocked, without editing each pod spec individually
Every pod automatically gets a Falco rule watching its system calls
Every pod's container image is automatically rescanned by Trivy before it starts
Every pod is automatically granted a workload identity
questions.explain: Lesson 21 is explicit that the Restricted Pod Security Standard, applied at the namespace level via a label, enforces non-root execution, drops all Linux capabilities by default, requires a seccomp profile, and blocks privilege escalation outright — for every pod in that namespace, without touching individual pod definitions.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23, Falco is built on ________, a Linux kernel technology that lets Falco's sensors observe system calls efficiently, without modifying the kernel.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 names eBPF as the kernel technology underlying Falco, letting it watch live system calls from every running container and evaluate them against a rule set in real time.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about securing CI/CD pipelines, per Lesson 22.
options: Pinning a third-party GitHub Action to a specific commit SHA, rather than a mutable tag, prevents its behavior from silently changing underneath you
A GitHub Actions environment can require approval from a named reviewer before a deploy job targeting it is allowed to run
Bypassing a deployment protection rule in GitHub Actions is always a silent, unlogged action
A pipeline with standing access to deploy and pull secrets is itself a meaningful attack surface, separate from anything it builds
Required reviewers make every other Chapter 4 scan unnecessary once they're configured
questions.explain: Lesson 22 recommends pinning actions by commit SHA and configuring required reviewers on sensitive environments, and frames the pipeline itself as a target precisely because of its standing access. It specifically contrasts this with a silent bypass: GitHub Actions makes bypassing a waiting protection rule a visible, logged action ("Start all waiting jobs"), not a silent skip — and required reviewers are one layer among several, not a replacement for Chapter 4's scans.

questions.code:
FROM node:20 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci && npm run build

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
COPY --from=build /app/dist /app
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server.js"]
questions.prompt: Put these pieces of Northbridge Retail's hardened checkout-service Dockerfile (Lesson 20) in the order they appear, from the first build stage to the final running process.
items: FROM node:20 AS build — the build stage starts from a full Node image
RUN npm ci && npm run build — dependencies install and the application compiles
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12 — the final stage starts from a minimal distroless image
COPY --from=build /app/dist /app — only the compiled output is copied into the final image
USER nonroot — the container process runs as a dedicated non-root user
questions.explain: Lesson 20's multi-stage build compiles everything in a full-featured build stage, then starts a clean, minimal final stage, copies in only the finished output, and runs it as non-root — keeping build tools, source code, and compilers out of the image that actually ships.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 25, what real gap does compliance as code close that a traditional, manual quarterly compliance review leaves open?
options: A system can drift out of compliance the day after a manual review passes, and nobody finds out until the next audit cycle — compliance as code catches that drift continuously instead
Manual audits are more technically accurate than automated controls, so compliance as code mainly just saves paperwork
Compliance as code fully replaces the need for a qualified PCI-DSS assessor
Manual audits can only ever check encryption settings, while compliance as code can only check logging settings
questions.explain: Lesson 25's core argument is that the gap between audits, not the audit itself, is the problem — a server can drift out of compliance the day after passing a manual review. Running the same check daily or on every change means the result is never more than a day stale, and the lesson is explicit that this produces continuous evidence, not a replacement for a formal assessor.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: tracking and monitoring all access to cardholder data and the systems that touch it is specifically PCI-DSS Requirement ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 26 ties audit logging directly to PCI-DSS Requirement 10, which requires tracking and monitoring all access to cardholder data and related systems — the reason Northbridge Retail's Activity Log has to capture every read, write, and permission change on resources touching payment data.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, per Lesson 28.
options: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery are grouped as one phase because they often happen in overlapping, iterative steps rather than strictly in sequence
Post-Incident Activity feeds back into Preparation, making the lifecycle a loop rather than a one-way line
Detection and Analysis is where audit logs, alerts, and scan findings get correlated into a single picture
Post-Incident Activity is optional paperwork once the immediate incident is resolved
Preparation only matters after an organization's first real incident has already occurred
questions.explain: Lesson 28 groups Containment, Eradication, and Recovery together precisely because they overlap in practice, and frames the whole lifecycle as a loop: Post-Incident Activity's lessons feed back into Preparation, which happens before any incident, not after the first one. Treating Post-Incident Activity as skippable paperwork, the lesson warns, throws away the phase that makes future incidents cheaper to handle.

questions.prompt: Match each NIST SP 800-61 phase to Northbridge Retail's corresponding action in Lesson 28's walkthrough of a suspected payment-data incident.
right: Azure Monitor audit logging, an on-call rotation, and a written incident response plan are already in place
The on-call engineer correlates an unusual read-volume alert against the Activity Log and classifies it as a high-severity incident
The team disables the implicated identity's credentials, rotates the leaked API key, and restores service with a freshly scoped identity
A retrospective documents how the key leaked and produces a new secrets-scanning rule plus a newly tuned alert
questions.explain: Lesson 28 walks a suspected incident through all four phases: Preparation is the logging, on-call rotation, and plan already in place beforehand; Detection and Analysis is correlating the anomalous alert against the Activity Log; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery is disabling credentials, rotating the key, and restoring service; Post-Incident Activity is the retrospective that produces concrete changes feeding back into Preparation.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 29, why is skipping one of the capstone's six required controls not simply "a smaller project"?
options: Because each control catches a category of problem none of the others do, so skipping one leaves that entire category uncovered rather than just reducing coverage a bit
Because the six controls must run in a fixed order, so skipping any one breaks the pipeline's syntax
Because AWS requires exactly six controls for any pipeline that's eligible for production traffic
Because the six controls are interchangeable, so skipping one is automatically compensated for by the others
questions.explain: Lesson 29 ties this directly back to Lesson 4's cumulative security principle: each of the six controls — SAST, dependency scanning, secrets scanning, image scanning, the policy gate, and least-privilege deploy identity — catches a category of problem the others structurally cannot, so skipping one isn't a smaller version of the same protection, it's a real gap.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the capstone pipeline's design, per Lessons 29 and 30.
options: The secrets scan runs first in stage order, because a leaked credential is the cheapest possible catch and the most urgent to block immediately
The policy gate is the single checkpoint that evaluates all prior scan results together before a deploy is allowed
order-service's least-privilege deploy identity names Key Vault read access, log write access, and deploy permission to its own environment, and nothing else
The image scan runs before the build stage, since it has to scan the image before it exists
A known-unfixable, low-exploitability finding must always block the deploy with absolutely no exceptions
questions.explain: Lesson 30 orders the pipeline secrets-scan, sast, dependency-scan, build, image-scan, policy-gate, deploy — the image scan necessarily runs after the build, not before, since it scans the freshly built image. The policy gate evaluates every prior result together, and the lesson's own precise gate rule explicitly allows excluding a known-unfixable, low-exploitability finding rather than blocking shipping forever.

questions.code:
stages:
  - secrets-scan     # block on any detected credential
  - sast              # block on critical/high finding
  - dependency-scan   # block on critical CVE, no fix available excluded
  - build             # compile + build container image
  - image-scan        # block on critical CVE in image layers
  - policy-gate        # evaluate all prior stage results together
  - deploy             # least-privilege workload identity only
questions.prompt: Put these stages of the capstone's order-service pipeline (Lesson 30) in the correct run order.
items: secrets-scan — block on any detected credential
sast — block on a critical or high finding
dependency-scan — block on a critical CVE, excluding ones with no fix available
build — compile order-service and build its container image
image-scan — block on a critical CVE found in the image's layers
policy-gate — evaluate all prior stage results together
deploy — using order-service's least-privilege deploy identity only
questions.explain: Lesson 30 orders every stage so the cheapest, earliest checks run first: secrets scanning catches the most urgent problem on every commit before anything else runs, SAST and dependency scanning check source and packages before a build exists, the build only happens after those pass, the image scan checks the freshly built artifact, the policy gate evaluates everything together, and deploy only happens last, under the least-privilege identity.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 31, what's the actual difference between a capstone pipeline that "works" and one that's "explainable" in an interview?
options: Explainable means being able to justify why each design decision was made — like why the policy gate threshold is CVSS 9.0 — not just that the pipeline runs without errors
Explainable means the pipeline's YAML is syntactically perfect, with zero formatting issues
Explainable means the pipeline is implemented in a specific named CI/CD vendor's tool rather than pseudocode
Explainable and working are the same thing — a pipeline that runs is automatically explainable
questions.explain: Lesson 31 draws this distinction directly: an interviewer isn't primarily checking whether the YAML is syntactically valid, but whether you can explain why the secrets scan runs before the build stage, why the gate threshold is CVSS 9.0 and not some other number, and why the deploy identity lists exactly three permissions — the reasoning behind the design, not just a working artifact.
